cse-1991-a-1-i.approach: Treat every MOS transistor as a switch: an nMOS conducts when its gate is 1, a pMOS (bubble) when its gate is 0. A series chain passes its input only when all its switches are on, and the two chains are wired together at $f$.

steps.title: Upper path (from x)
steps.body: pMOS with gate $a$ conducts when $a=0$; nMOS with gate $b$ conducts when $b=1$. In series both must be on, so $x$ reaches $f$ when $\overline{a}\,b = 1$: contribution $\overline{a}\,b\,x$.

steps.title: Lower path (from y)
steps.body: nMOS with gate $a$ conducts when $a=1$; pMOS with gate $b$ conducts when $b=0$. So $y$ reaches $f$ when $a\,\overline{b}=1$: contribution $a\,\overline{b}\,y$.

steps.title: Combine at f
steps.body:
The two conditions $\overline{a}b$ and $a\overline{b}$ are mutually exclusive, so at most one path drives $f$ (no conflict):

$$f = \overline{a}\,b\,x + a\,\overline{b}\,y$$

(When $a=b$ neither path conducts and $f$ floats.)

pitfalls: Reading the bubble as a NOT on the data path — it marks a pMOS gate (on at logic 0).
Writing an XOR of $a,b$ only: the data inputs $x$ and $y$ must appear.
cse-1991-a-1-i.verification: Check $a=0,b=1$: upper chain on, lower off ⇒ $f=x$; formula gives $1\cdot x+0=x$. $a=1,b=0$: $f=y$. ✓

cse-1991-a-1-ii.approach: Look at which address bits select the module. If the low-order bits pick the module, consecutive addresses land in consecutive modules; if the high-order bits pick it, a whole block of consecutive addresses lives in one module.

steps.title: Low-order interleaving
steps.body: With $2^m$ modules, module $=$ address $\bmod 2^m$ (the lowest $m$ bits). Words $0,1,2,3,\dots$ go to modules $0,1,2,3,\dots$ — consecutive words in **consecutive modules**, enabling pipelined/parallel access.

steps.title: High-order interleaving
steps.body: Module $=$ the top $m$ address bits. Module 0 holds addresses $0 \dots N-1$, module 1 the next block, so consecutive words stay **within the same module**.

pitfalls: Swapping the two: high-order interleaving does not spread consecutive words across modules.
cse-1991-a-1-ii.verification: 4 modules, 16 words: low-order puts word 5 in module $5 \bmod 4 = 1$ and word 6 in module 2; high-order puts words 4–7 all in module 1. ✓

cse-1991-a-1-iii.approach: Add the terms exactly as printed and convert the total to binary, splitting it into powers of two.

steps.title: Count the 1s
steps.body: Four distinct powers of two ⇒ **4** ones.

pitfalls: Reading the expression as hex digits $9,7,5,3$ in positions — the terms are simply added.

cse-1991-a-1-iv.approach: The 8087 coprocessor shares the local bus with the 8086 and needs the queue-status (QS0/QS1) and RQ/GT lines, which the 8086 provides only in maximum mode.

steps.title: What the 8087 needs
steps.body: The 8087 tracks the 8086 instruction queue via **QS0, QS1** and requests the bus via **$\overline{RQ}/\overline{GT}$**. It also relies on the 8288 bus controller for bus commands.

steps.title: Which mode supplies them
steps.body: Those pins exist only when $MN/\overline{MX} = 0$, i.e. **maximum mode** (multiprocessor configuration). In minimum mode the same pins carry ALE, $\overline{INTA}$, HOLD/HLDA instead.

pitfalls: Minimum mode is for single-processor systems; it lacks QS0/QS1 and RQ/GT.
cse-1991-a-1-iv.verification: Intel 8086 data sheet: coprocessor (8087) and I/O-processor (8089) configurations are maximum-mode configurations. ✓

cse-1991-a-1-v.approach: Write the long multiplication: column 0 has one partial product, column 1 has two. The product bit is the XOR (sum bit) of the column's partial products, since column 0 produces no carry.

steps.title: Partial products by column
steps.body:
Column 0: $a_0b_0$ only ⇒ $c_0 = a_0b_0$ with no carry.

Column 1: $a_1b_0$ and $a_0b_1$.

steps.title: Add column 1
steps.body:
A half adder adds the two bits: sum $= a_1b_0 \oplus a_0b_1$, carry $= a_1b_0\,a_0b_1$ goes to column 2.

$$c_1 = a_1b_0 \oplus a_0b_1$$

pitfalls: Using OR instead of XOR: when both partial products are 1, $c_1 = 0$ and a carry goes up.

cse-1991-a-1-vi.approach: Find a property true on loop entry and preserved by one iteration. The guard $i \bmod 2 = 0$ makes $i$ even on entry, and the body always corrects the parity back to even.

steps.title: Initially
steps.body: The while-loop is reached only if $i \bmod 2 = 0$, so $i$ is even at the first test.

steps.title: One iteration preserves it
steps.body:
Let $j = i \text{ div } 2$.
- If $j$ is odd, $i := j - 1$ — odd minus 1 is even.
- If $j$ is even, $i := j - 2$ — even minus 2 is even.

Either way $i$ is even before the next test.

steps.title: Invariant
steps.body: At every evaluation of the loop condition, $i \bmod 2 = 0$ ($i$ is even).

pitfalls: Stating $i \ge 0$ — that is the loop guard, not an invariant (it fails on exit).
cse-1991-a-1-vi.verification: Trace $i = 12$: $12\to 6\to 4$ (6 even ⇒ $-2$), $4 \to 2 \to 0$, $0 \to 0 \to -2$ — every value at the test (12, 4, 0, −2) is even. ✓

cse-1991-a-1-vii.approach: Use the decision-tree lower bound $\lceil \log_2 n! \rceil$ and note that for $n = 5$ the Ford–Johnson (merge-insertion) method meets it.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: A comparison sort must distinguish $5! = 120$ orderings, and a binary decision tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves. $2^6 = 64 < 120 \le 128 = 2^7$, so $h \ge \lceil\log_2 120\rceil = 7$.

steps.title: Achievability
steps.body: Merge-insertion: compare $(a,b)$, $(c,d)$ (2), compare the winners (3) giving chain $a<b<d$ with $c<d$; insert $e$ into $a<b<d$ by binary search (2 more ⇒ 5); insert $c$ into the elements below $d$ (at most 3 items) with 2 comparisons ⇒ **7** total.

pitfalls: Quoting $n\log_2 n \approx 11.6$ or the merge-sort worst case (8) instead of the optimum.

cse-1991-a-1-viii.approach: Weighted external path length $= \sum (\text{weight of leaf}) \times (\text{depth of leaf})$, depth counted in edges from the root. Group leaves by depth and add.
pitfalls: Counting depth in nodes (root = 1) — that adds the total weight 52 and gives 196.
cse-1991-a-1-viii.verification: Equivalent check: WEPL = sum of the internal-node weights (each internal node = sum of leaves below it): $6 + 12 + 18 + 19 + 37 + 52 = 144$ ✓.

cse-1991-a-1-ix.approach: Inorder = (left subtree, node, right subtree), applied recursively. Node 3 has only a right child, so it is visited before its right subtree.

steps.title: Left subtree of 7
steps.body: Subtree rooted at 1 with children 4 and 6: inorder gives $4, 1, 6$.

steps.title: Root
steps.body: The left subtree is finished, so the root $7$ is visited next.

steps.title: Right subtree of 7
steps.body: Node 3 has no left child, so visit $3$ first, then its right subtree rooted at 5: $2, 5, 8$.

pitfalls: Treating 5 as the left child of 3 — it is the right child, so 3 comes before 2, 5, 8.
cse-1991-a-1-ix.verification: Count: 8 nodes listed once each; the root 7 splits them into its left subtree {4,1,6} and right subtree {3,2,5,8} ✓.

cse-1991-a-1-x.approach: Let $C(n)$ be the number of calls made when evaluating fib(n), including itself. Each call with $n\ge2$ makes one call to fib(n−1) and one to fib(n−2), giving a Fibonacci-like recurrence.
pitfalls: Counting only additions (20) or only leaf calls (21) instead of all calls.
cse-1991-a-1-x.verification: The recursion tree has $F(7) = 21$ leaves (each returns 1) and is full binary, so it has $21 - 1 = 20$ internal calls: $21 + 20 = 41$ ✓.

cse-1991-a-1-xi.approach: Every variable $a\dots f$ must be read from memory at least once, so 6 operand accesses is a lower bound; reach it by keeping all intermediates in registers and evaluating the deeper (right) subtree first, Sethi–Ullman style, which needs only 2 registers.

steps.title: Expression tree
steps.body:
`**` binds tightest, then `*`, `/`, then `-`:
$$((a+b)\cdot c) - (d / e^{f})$$
The right operand $d/e^f$ is the deeper subtree, so evaluate it first.

steps.title: Code with 2 registers
steps.body:
```
MOV  R1, e      ; R1 = e
POW  R1, f      ; R1 = e**f
MOV  R2, d      ; R2 = d
DIV  R2, R1     ; R2 = d / e**f
MOV  R1, a      ; R1 = a
ADD  R1, b      ; R1 = a + b
MUL  R1, c      ; R1 = (a+b)*c
SUB  R1, R2     ; R1 = result
```
Memory operands read: $e, f, d, a, b, c$ — **6**, each exactly once.

steps.title: Why not 1 register
steps.body: $d / e^f$ needs $d$ as the destination, so $d$ must sit in a register while $e^f$ is held in another (or spilled, costing extra memory accesses). Hence 2 registers is the minimum that achieves 6 accesses.

pitfalls: Evaluating $(a+b)\cdot c$ first: its value then occupies a register while $d/e^f$ needs two more ⇒ 3 registers.
If the final result must also be written to memory, add one store (7 accesses).
cse-1991-a-1-xi.verification: Sethi–Ullman labels (left leaf 1, right leaf 0): $e^f = 1$; $d/e^f$ has children 1 and 1 ⇒ 2; $a+b = 1$, $(a+b)c = 1$; root has children 1 and 2 ⇒ $\max = 2$ registers ✓.

cse-1991-a-1-xii.approach: parbegin/parend can only express nested compositions of sequence and parallel blocks, so exactly the precedence graphs that decompose that way (series–parallel / properly nested graphs) are expressible.

steps.title: What the construct builds
steps.body: `begin S1; S2 end` composes in **series**; `parbegin S1; S2 parend` composes in **parallel**. Nesting these gives only series–parallel structures.

steps.title: Consequence
steps.body: A precedence graph is implementable with parbegin/parend alone iff it is **properly nested (series–parallel)**. Graphs like $S_1\to S_3$, $S_1\to S_4$, $S_2\to S_4$ (an "N" shape) are not, and need fork/join or semaphores.

pitfalls: Answering "acyclic": every precedence graph is a DAG, but not every DAG is series–parallel.
cse-1991-a-1-xii.verification: Standard result (Shaw / Silberschatz, "Concurrent statements"): parbegin–parend graphs are exactly the properly nested graphs ✓.

cse-1991-a-1-xiii.approach: Each residue class mod 3 has exactly 100 members in $1..300$. Fix $i$ and $j$ freely; then $k$ must lie in one specific residue class.

steps.title: Residues are balanced
steps.body: $1..300$ contains 100 numbers $\equiv 0$, 100 $\equiv 1$ and 100 $\equiv 2 \pmod 3$.

steps.title: Choose i, j, then k
steps.body:
$i$: 300 choices, $j$: 300 choices. For $i+j+k \equiv 0$, $k \equiv -(i+j) \pmod 3$ — exactly 100 choices.
$$300 \times 300 \times 100 = 9\,000\,000$$

pitfalls: Counting only $i\equiv j\equiv k$ cases ($3\cdot100^3 = 3\times10^6$) and forgetting the $(0,1,2)$ permutations ($6\cdot100^3$).
cse-1991-a-1-xiii.verification: By cases: all same residue $3\cdot10^6$ + all different $3!\cdot10^6 = 6\cdot10^6$ ⇒ $9\cdot10^6$ ✓, which is $\tfrac13$ of $300^3 = 2.7\times10^7$.

cse-1991-a-1-xiv.approach: Mirsky's theorem (dual of Dilworth): if the longest chain has $n$ elements, the poset can be partitioned into $n$ antichains, by grouping elements by the length of the longest chain ending at them.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body: For each $x$, let $h(x)$ = number of elements in the longest chain whose maximum is $x$; $1 \le h(x) \le n$. Put $A_t = \{x : h(x) = t\}$.

steps.title: Each level is an antichain
steps.body: If $x < y$ then any chain ending at $x$ extends by $y$, so $h(y) > h(x)$. Hence two comparable elements never share a level: each $A_t$ is an antichain, and $A_1, \dots, A_n$ form a **disjoint union (partition)** of the poset.

pitfalls: Confusing with Dilworth (width ⇒ partition into chains).
cse-1991-a-1-xiv.verification: Divisors of 12 under "divides": longest chain 1|2|4|12 has 4 elements; levels {1}, {2,3}, {4,6}, {12} are 4 antichains ✓.

cse-1991-a-1-xv.approach: To maximise edges, make $k-1$ components isolated vertices and put the remaining $n-k+1$ vertices in one complete graph — moving vertices into the biggest component only increases the edge count.

steps.title: Why one big component
steps.body: If components have sizes $p \ge q \ge 2$ (both complete), moving one vertex from the smaller to the larger changes edges by $p - (q-1) \ge 1 > 0$. So the optimum has one component of size $n-k+1$ and $k-1$ singletons.

pitfalls: Splitting vertices evenly among the $k$ components — that minimises, not maximises, the complete-graph edges.

cse-1991-a-2-i.approach: Recall what each standard is: IEEE-488 is GPIB (instruments), IEEE-796 is Intel Multibus (backplane), IEEE-696 is the S-100 bus, RS-232-C is a point-to-point serial link.

steps.title: Identify each
steps.body:
| Standard | What it is | Match |
|---|---|---|
| IEEE 488 | General Purpose Interface Bus for test instruments | R |
| IEEE 796 | Intel **Multibus** backplane | S |
| IEEE 696 | S-100 system bus linking CPU and other boards | Q |
| RS-232-C | serial link to a single device (terminal, modem) | P |

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Reading the match column top to bottom: A–R, B–S, C–Q, D–P (each List II item used once).

pitfalls: Mixing up 796 (Multibus) and 696 (S-100).
cse-1991-a-2-i.verification: Each list II entry used exactly once ✓; only RS-232 is a single-device point-to-point link.

cse-1991-a-2-ii.approach: Recall each 8086 pin function: RQ/GT and LOCK are maximum-mode pins, HOLD is the minimum-mode DMA request, READY inserts wait states.

steps.title: Pin functions
steps.body:
| Pin | Function | Match |
|---|---|---|
| $\overline{RQ}/\overline{GT}$ | request/grant of the local bus by another master in **maximum mode** | R |
| $\overline{LOCK}$ | processor keeps the bus across consecutive cycles (LOCK prefix) | P |
| HOLD | bus request from a DMA device in **minimum mode** | S |
| READY | slow memory/I-O extends the cycle with wait states | Q |

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Reading the match column top to bottom: A–R, B–P, C–S, D–Q (each List II item used once).

pitfalls: Swapping RQ/GT and HOLD: HOLD/HLDA exist only in minimum mode.
cse-1991-a-2-ii.verification: In maximum mode pins 30/31 become $\overline{RQ}/\overline{GT_0}$, $\overline{RQ}/\overline{GT_1}$ — the same pins that are HLDA/HOLD in minimum mode ✓.

cse-1991-a-2-iii.approach: Pair each concept with the area it belongs to: buddy system is an allocator, interpreters can check types at run time, virtual memory is realised by paging/segmentation, pointer types create unreachable heap cells that need garbage collection.

steps.title: Match
steps.body:
| List I | Reason | List II |
|---|---|---|
| Buddy system | splits/merges power-of-two blocks | R. Memory allocation |
| Interpretation | types bound and checked while executing | P. Run-time type specification |
| Virtual memory | implemented via segmentation (or paging) | Q. Segmentation |
| Pointer type | heap objects can become unreachable | S. Garbage collection |

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Reading the match column top to bottom: A–R, B–P, C–Q, D–S (each List II item used once).

pitfalls: Linking garbage collection to the buddy system — the buddy system frees explicitly; GC is needed because pointers make reachability dynamic.
cse-1991-a-2-iii.verification: Each list II item is used exactly once and every pairing is a textbook association ✓.

cse-1991-a-2-iv.approach: Recognise each count: Catalan number, central binomial, half of $n!$, and a palindrome determined by its first half.

steps.title: A and B
steps.body:
(A) Binary trees with $n$ nodes: Catalan $C_n = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ ⇒ **S**.

(B) Length $2n$ with $n$ zeros: choose zero positions $\binom{2n}{n}$ ⇒ **R**.

steps.title: Part C
steps.body: For $n \ge 2$, exactly half of the $n!$ permutations are even (multiplying by a fixed transposition is a bijection between even and odd ones) ⇒ $\frac{n!}{2}$ ⇒ **P**.

steps.title: Part D
steps.body: A palindrome of length $6n$ is fixed by its first $3n$ symbols; $2n$ zeros overall means $n$ zeros in the first half. Choose them: $\binom{3n}{n}$ ⇒ **Q**.

pitfalls: For D, choosing $2n$ zeros among $6n$ positions ignores the palindrome constraint.
cse-1991-a-2-iv.verification: $n=2$: binary trees with 2 nodes = 2 = $\frac13\binom42$ ✓; strings 0011-type = $\binom42 = 6$ ✓; even perms of 2 objects = 1 = $2!/2$ ✓.

cse-1991-a-3-i.approach: In static CMOS either the pull-up or the pull-down network is off in steady state, so no DC current flows — its decisive advantage. It costs more transistors, area and masks.

steps.title: Power
steps.body: nMOS logic uses a depletion load: when the output is LOW a DC path exists from $V_{DD}$ to ground. CMOS has complementary networks, only one conducting in steady state, so static power ≈ 0 ⇒ **lower power dissipation**.

steps.title: Other claims
steps.body: CMOS needs a pMOS for every nMOS (2 transistors per input) plus an n-well, so chips are larger and need **more** masks. Speed was not CMOS's classic advantage — pMOS devices are slower (lower hole mobility) and gates have more input capacitance.

optionAnalysis.reason: Complementary networks ⇒ no static current path ⇒ far lower power.
Not the defining advantage: pMOS pull-ups and doubled gate capacitance offset gains; 1991-era nMOS was comparable or faster.
CMOS needs about twice the transistors plus wells ⇒ larger area.
Wells and dual implants need extra masks, not fewer.

pitfalls: Assuming CMOS is smaller because modern chips are CMOS — density comes from scaling, not from CMOS vs nMOS.
cse-1991-a-3-i.verification: Standard VLSI texts (Weste–Eshraghian) list near-zero static power as the key CMOS advantage ✓.

cse-1991-a-3-ii.approach: A clock makes state change only at defined instants after signals settle, so transient glitches (hazards) and races do not matter — the main design advantage. Speed and hardware economy favour asynchronous circuits.

steps.title: Why hazards are easy to avoid
steps.body: Flip-flops sample inputs only at the clock edge. As long as the clock period exceeds the worst combinational delay, glitches in the next-state logic die out before sampling — no hazard-free covers or race analysis needed.

steps.title: Check the rest
steps.body: Asynchronous circuits are not slowed by a worst-case clock (faster) and need no clock distribution or flip-flops (less hardware). Noise immunity is a property of the logic family, not of clocking.

answer.value: B — ease of avoiding problems due to hazards

optionAnalysis.reason: Clocking forces worst-case timing; asynchronous circuits are potentially faster.
Edge-triggered sampling ignores glitches and races, avoiding hazard problems.
Synchronous designs add flip-flops and clock circuitry — more hardware.
Noise margins depend on the logic family (TTL, CMOS), not on synchronous vs asynchronous design.

pitfalls: Choosing "faster" — that is the classic advantage of asynchronous circuits.
cse-1991-a-3-ii.verification: Textbooks (Mano, Kohavi) cite hazard/race-free operation and easier design as the reason synchronous circuits dominate ✓.

cse-1991-a-3-iii.approach: The size of the virtual address space is $2^{k}$ where $k$ is the width of the address the CPU generates (held in the MAR in the textbook model). Main memory only limits how much is resident at once.

steps.title: Address width sets the space
steps.body: With a $k$-bit address register the CPU can name only $2^k$ distinct locations, so the total virtual address space is bounded by the length of the MAR (address bits).

steps.title: Why not main/secondary memory
steps.body: Virtual memory exists precisely so the address space can exceed main memory (C is wrong). Secondary storage limits how much of the space can actually be backed, but the *size of the address space* itself is fixed by the address length; hence "all of the above" also fails.

optionAnalysis.reason: A $k$-bit address can name only $2^k$ locations, fixing the address-space size.
Secondary storage limits how many pages can be backed (usable space), not how large the address space is; some sources still accept it.
Virtual memory lets the address space exceed main memory.
Main memory is clearly not a limit, so "all" is false.

pitfalls: Confusing address-space size with the amount of memory actually usable.
cse-1991-a-3-iii.verification: E.g. 32-bit addresses ⇒ 4 GB virtual space regardless of RAM size; this matches the stored key A (flagged for review because B is argued by some solvers).
